questions.solution_text:
The condition is $C$, so the sample space is reduced to the $5 + 13 = 18$ students in $C$.
Of those $18$, the $5$ in the overlap are left-handed.
$P(L \mid C) = \frac{n(L \cap C)}{n(C)}$
$= \frac{5}{18}$

questions.question_text:
The two-way table shows the lunch orders placed by $72$ students at a school canteen.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Year 7} & \text{Year 8} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Hot food} & 24 & 12 & 36 \\ \text{Sandwich} & 16 & 20 & 36 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 40 & 32 & 72 \end{array}$
One order is chosen at random.
Find the probability that it is hot food, given that it was placed by a Year $8$ student, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Divided the $12$ by the hot food row total of $36$, which reverses the condition and gives $P(\text{Year } 8 \mid \text{hot food})$.
Used the grand total of $72$ as the denominator instead of the Year $8$ column total.
Gave the unconditional probability of a Year $8$ order by using $32$ out of $72$.

questions.solution_text:
The condition restricts the sample space to the Year $8$ column, whose total is $32$.
Of those $32$ orders, $12$ are hot food.
$P(\text{hot food} \mid \text{Year } 8) = \frac{12}{32}$
$= \frac{3}{8}$

questions.question_text:
In a class of $32$ students, $20$ walk to school, $14$ have a part-time job and $9$ both walk and have a part-time job.
One student is chosen at random.
Find the probability that the student walks to school, given that they have a part-time job, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Conditioned on walking instead of on having a job, so this is $P(\text{job} \mid \text{walks})$.
Used the whole class of $32$ as the denominator instead of reducing the sample space to the job holders.
Gave the unconditional probability of having a part-time job, $14$ out of $32$, ignoring the condition.

questions.solution_text:
The condition is 'has a part-time job', so the sample space is reduced to those $14$ students.
Of those $14$, the $9$ who also walk are favourable.
$P(\text{walks} \mid \text{job}) = \frac{9}{14}$

questions.question_text:
In a class of $30$ students, $18$ catch the bus to school, $12$ have a part-time job and $6$ do both.
Let $B$ be the event 'the student catches the bus' and $J$ be the event 'the student has a part-time job'.
One student is chosen at random. Find $P(B \mid J)$ as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Divided by the $18$ bus catchers instead of the $12$ job holders, reversing the event and condition to give $P(J \mid B)$.
Divided the $6$ students in both events by the whole class of $30$, ignoring the condition.
Used the $18$ bus catchers out of the whole class of $30$, giving the unconditional $P(B)$.

questions.solution_text:
The condition is $J$, so the sample space is reduced to the $12$ students with a part-time job.
Of those $12$, $6$ catch the bus.
$P(B \mid J) = \frac{6}{12}$
$= \frac{1}{2}$

options.why: Divided by $n(J)=15$ instead of $n(B)=24$, reversing the condition to give $P(B \mid J)$.
Divided the $8$ students in both events by the whole survey of $36$, ignoring the condition.
Used all $15$ job holders as the numerator over the $24$ bus catchers, including job holders outside the condition.

questions.solution_text:
The condition is $B$, so the sample space is reduced to the $8 + 16 = 24$ bus catchers.
Of those $24$, the $8$ in the overlap have a part-time job.
$P(J \mid B) = \frac{8}{24}$
$= \frac{1}{3}$

questions.question_text:
At a large school, $P(B) = 0.4$, $P(J) = 0.25$ and $P(J \cap B) = 0.14$, where $B$ is 'a student catches the bus to school' and $J$ is 'a student has a part-time job'.
Find $P(J \mid B)$ as a decimal.

options.why: Divided by $P(J)$ instead of $P(B)$, which reverses the condition and gives $P(B \mid J)$.
Stopped at the intersection probability without dividing by the probability of the condition.
Gave the unconditional $P(J)$, ignoring the reduction of the sample space to $B$.

questions.solution_text:
The condition is $B$, so the denominator is $P(B)$.
$P(J \mid B) = \frac{P(J \cap B)}{P(B)}$
$= \frac{0.14}{0.4}$
$= 0.35$

questions.question_text:
At a large school, $30\%$ of students are left-handed and $60\%$ catch the bus to school.
Being left-handed and catching the bus are independent events.
Find $P(L \mid B)$ as a percentage, where $L$ is 'the student is left-handed' and $B$ is 'the student catches the bus'.

options.why: Swapped the event and the condition, giving $P(B \mid L)$ rather than $P(L \mid B)$.
Divided $30\%$ by $60\%$ as though $P(L)$ were the intersection probability.
Multiplied $30\%$ by $60\%$, which gives $P(L \cap B)$ rather than the conditional probability.

questions.solution_text:
The events are independent, so knowing that a student catches the bus gives no new information about being left-handed.
The bus catchers contain the same proportion of left-handed students as the whole school.
$P(L \mid B) = P(L)$
$= 30\%$

questions.question_text:
In a survey of $48$ students, $30$ catch the bus to school, $22$ have a part-time job and $8$ do neither.
One student is chosen at random.
Find the probability that the student has a part-time job, given that they catch the bus, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Divided the $12$ in both events by the $22$ job holders, which reverses the condition and gives $P(B \mid J)$.
Used the whole survey of $48$ as the denominator instead of reducing it to the bus catchers.
Gave the unconditional probability of having a part-time job, $22$ out of $48$.

questions.question_text:
For two events $M$ and $N$, $P(M)=0.3$, $P(N)=0.5$ and $P(M\cap N)=0.2$.
Since $P(N)>0$, $P(M\mid N)$ is defined. Find $P(M\mid N)$ as a decimal.

options.why: Used the intersection probability without dividing by the probability of the condition.
Divided $0.2$ by $P(M)=0.3$ instead of $P(N)=0.5$, reversing the condition, then rounded to two decimal places.
Used the unconditional $P(M)$, ignoring the condition.

questions.solution_text:
The condition is $N$, whose probability is $0.5>0$.
$P(M\mid N)=\frac{P(M\cap N)}{P(N)}$
$=\frac{0.2}{0.5}$
$=0.4$
